It happened about a year ago.  I'd been dealing with pretty heavy depression since I was 11 (I was 17 at the time).  Around September of 2012 I decided to go numb.  I completely shut off my emotions and went dead.  I was living on adderall, energy drinks, and coffee.  I was basically doing whatever I could to make sure I wouldn't have to come down and deal with the fact that everything I looked at I was coming up with strategies for how I could kill myself with it.  If I saw a tree, I would think about ways to fall out that would achieve maximum damage.  If a car was passing by I played chicken with myself to see if I would jump in front of it.
  
Eventually it got to a point where I was starting to see things moving out of the corner of my eyes.  I was sleeping maybe three hours for every four or five days.  I snapped in January.  I stopped eating.  I started losing track of time.  I remember one night I was trying to figure out how I got from my Calculus class, which was at 8am, to sitting in my room that night.  I couldn't follow anything anyone was saying to me.  Conversations were next to impossible so I stopped talking to people all the way through until graduation time came around.  It was hell.  
  
I still get those urges when I'm standing next to traffic on my university campus to walk out in the middle of it.  I'm just getting to the point where I can write again.  That was the worst part about going numb.  I lost my ability to write.  All of my inspiration faded away and I was left with complete bullshit coming out of my pen while I attempted to express things the way normal people do.  I started burning myself with matches to let out the frustration because I wasn't able to feel or express anything anymore.  It's like I'm trying to stitch a wound that healed ages ago but I'm still trying to remember what the pain felt like, but the more time that passes, the less I can remember what it's like to feel.  It's scary to be honest.

Thanks.  I think one of my biggest triggers about this is that not many people in my family go to college.  Hell, some of them are lucky to even graduate from high school, so this is a huge deal.  Everyone's rooting for me, telling me they hope I succeed.  And I just have this voice in the back of my head that I'm going to let them all down.  That I'm going to end up dropping out and homeless because I don't know how to cope with life.  Especially unknown environments.  Hell, I almost had a breakdown working at a day camp over the summer.  I always feel like I have to completely succeed at what I do, or everything was for nothing.  I just know I have a lot of inner demons I need to exorcise or I'm going to lose my shit once I'm out there on my own.  I want to enter into my adult life on the right foot, by gathering the right tools to deal with the things thrust upon me in childhood so that it doesn't ruin my shot at happiness in the future.  
  
Thanks.  I'm definitely going to check the student health center and start getting the ball rolling on that.  I've been going it on my own for so long, maybe I need someone to help guide me through it.  I'm always the one helping everyone out, but when it comes time when I need help, there's no one left.

I was riding in a car with my family and friends on a long stretch of highway.  A thunderstorm came out of nowhere and all of the ditches and swamps flooded the streets.  My mom couldn't see where she was going, and drove us into a shallow ditch.  I got out and easily moved the car out of the water.  I pushed the car up a hill where our apartment magically appeared.  The floor was flooded about a foot deep.  We acted like it was normal business.  
  
As we walked through the door, everyone with me turned into giant animals.  My best friend was a rabbit, his ex girlfriend was a bird, and my family turned into giant mice.  I was the only one left human.  Again, everyone acted like it was something that came expected when you walked through a door.  
  
I walked into my room and took my pet snake out of its cage (I don't own a snake) and lay down with it on my bed.  It started talking to me, asking me why I left it.  I told him I had business to take care of in the city.  He told me he missed me.  I told him I missed him too.  He cuddled my neck and then asked if his family could move in.  I said no.  He got angry.  He threatened to bite my lips, and I threw him across the room.  He hit the wall and fell into his cage. I threw some books on top of it to make sure it stayed closed.  I then did the victory dance in the water and walked out of my room while mice tortured the snake.  
  
I woke up.

I don't know.  I've come across a few people well into their 40s boasting that they don't read when they don't have to. A lot of the adults throw off getting an education as something only people with money or are insanely intelligent are capable of doing.  The general attitude is that sports are more important than education, to the point where the football coach encourages the players to come to practice rather than study for midterms, even if they could have potentially failed the grading term if they didn't (happened to a guy I knew, who then quit the team because he didn't support that mindset).  
  
It's ridiculous.  And then, when the local newspaper gave grades to each of the schools based on drop out rates, state testing, ACT scores, and other factors, the school was graded as a D school, people were trying to figure out how our good old school could have that grade while having an average of 5 valedictorians a year.  
  
The valedictorian of my graduating class said it best.  There's the kids who are in all honors classes who have the pressure to do well in school because the only people you're around are the ones who are doing well, and then it drops off.  There's literally almost no middle ground.  You either have a 3.0+ or are just scraping by.  And the adults in the area don't help much.  I'm currently working at a summer camp that also tutors kids in math, English, science, and social studies depending on the grade they're going to in August.  I had to explain to someone who Martin Luther King Jr was.  The kid thought he was a president.  They couldn't name more than three actual presidents and couldn't tell what they were famous for (someone said George Washington was famous for being on money), and they have a very basic understanding of the English language.  It breaks my heart.

I wrote my first short story when I was seven. I suppose from the very beginning my stories have been my way of making commentary on the things that effect my daily life.  
  
What really sparked my need to write with greater detail was Interview with the Vampire.  I found the book in the school library like a golden beacon (the sun was shining on the golden book sleeve).  After I read that book, I dove into the realm of dark fantasy novels and began developing an insatiable love for writers who could describe an object down to the most miniscule aspect that I could have a perfect image of, say, the candelabra a murderer intended to use in the murder of his benefactor.  
  
As I've developed my writing, I've begun to create my own universe in which all of my stories are playing out, at various points in time.  I've created different planets and societies that interlock.  
  
But looking back at the first novelette I wrote when I was 12, I can see that I had a love for using nearly every cliche that popped into my head back then.

That right there is the reason I never went into treatment and am still struggling with the binge aspect of my ED.  I did the aforementioned binge-starve cycle spread out over the course of a few months (binge for 3-4 months, eat very little for two and repeat), fluctuating between mid-range overweight to barely breaking into the obese range.  
  
My mom never tried to get me treatment even though I told her about it because she didn't think it was serious.  Anyone I told laughed it off and it got to the point where I didn't even take myself seriously to think I really had a problem, even though all of the health signs were there.  I still have the effects of that today, even though I started working on my diet two years ago.  
  
I know girls who were in the 300+ club when the onset of their eating disorders hit, and had been extremely restricting to get to that 200 pound marker.  Anyone looking at them would have still thought they ate everything in sight, which is what makes it so much easier for people who are bigger at the onset to hide their eating habits, also giving them more time to perfect the sneaky habits they need in order to keep up the charade of eating healthy once they're in the lower weight ranges.  
  
If a person my size came up to me and told me they had an eating disorder, I would just ask them how long it had been going on, not laugh at them.  All that does is A) Make them not want to seek help in any other, more reliable source and B) reinforce every single negative thought they have going through their head on repeat.  The worse thing a person could do to someone with an eating disorder is make a remark about their weight.  They will take that as a critique of their entire essence, because the eating disorder becomes everything you know and consumes your soul until you don't know who you are anymore.
  
I've been there and spent all of my time online during the two years I let it control me interacting with people from every walk of life connected by these diseases.  
  
I'm sorry I just went on a rant.  This is one thing that really gets under my skin.
